Posted in: HBO, Max, Movies, Paramount+, TV | Tagged: paramount, Warner Bros
Warner Bros Antitrust Trial: Paramount Wants 2026, States Want 2027
Paramount Skydance wants a November 2026 trial date for the Warner Bros Discovery antitrust lawsuit, while the states want April 2027.
Article Summary
- Paramount Skydance wants a November 4, 2026 trial in the Warner Bros. Discovery antitrust case; states want April 5, 2027.
- The schedule fight matters: Paramount Skydance could owe Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders $7 million per day after Sept. 30.
- California AG Rob Bonta and 12 states say the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would raise prices and reduce content quality.
- Paramount argues the merger is lawful and pro-competitive, saying it would better position the company against Netflix and Big Tech.
In this corner, we have David Ellison's Paramount Skydance. The company is looking for a November 4th, 2026, date for the antitrust lawsuit filed by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and 12 states (California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Washington) as part of their lawsuit to block
"We believe a trial on the merits is the best and most direct way for us to prove what we've said from the start — this transaction is lawful, pro-competitive, and raises no antitrust concerns," a Paramount spokesperson said about the states' date filing. "Our request for a November trial date is more than sufficient to give both sides the time they need to conduct discovery, gather evidence, and prepare for trial." AG Bonta said in a statement, "Our challenge to the unlawful Warner Bros./Paramount merger is a clean-cut antitrust challenge through and through: it's about protecting the vibrancy of an industry, the pockets of consumers, and the quality of films and television programs that take center stage in many of our lives. This challenge deserves careful and thorough review and today my office and attorneys general across the country asked the court for a trial date next spring. We are eager to continue to make our case and look forward to a final determination of the schedule by the court."
Paramount Skydance, 12 States Make Their Arguments
"Today, I am leading a coalition of states in challenging the proposed merger of Warner Bros. and Paramount and asking the court to block the deal. The unlawful merger of these two entertainment behemoths would lead to higher prices, lower quality, and less content for film and television, harming movie theaters, basic cable distributors, and ultimately, audiences on every sofa and movie theater seat in the U.S.," shared Bonta in a statement.
He continued, "California's film and entertainment industry touches the lives of Americans daily – it comes into the living rooms of families, has a starring role in many young people's first dates, and is a point of immense pride and employment for Californians up and down our state. Consolidation here not only leads to higher prices – it also leads to fewer opportunities for important stories to come to life, and fewer ways for audiences to encounter stories, ideas, and perspectives beyond their own experiences. In this country, no one is above the law. With this lawsuit, California and our sister states are fighting for free and fair markets, not rigged markets. America has no kings in government or our economy."
Here's a look at what the lawsuit claims the proposed merger would be in violation of (and you can check out the entire press release from Bonta's office here):
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District for the Northern District of California, alleges that the merger violates Section 7 of the Clayton Act, which holds that mergers that may substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly are illegal. The attorneys general allege that, if Warner Bros. and Paramount are allowed to merge, it would lessen competition in the areas of:
- Wide Release Theatrical Film Distribution, where Warner Bros. and Paramount are two of the five major film distributors and would combine for around 27% share of the market. After the merger, only three distributors will control 75% of these films and only four distributors (Defendants, Disney, Universal, and Sony) will control 86% of them.
- Anticipated Top-Grossing Theatrical Film Distribution, a submarket of theatrical film distribution focused on anticipated blockbuster films with wide audiences and large production budgets. After the merger, Defendants will control more than 30% of these films, and four distributors (Defendants, Disney, Universal, and Sony) will control more than 90% of them.
- Licensing Basic Cable Television Channels, or the market for distributing basic cable channels to cable and satellite providers. Warner Bros. is the second largest and Paramount is the third largest in this market, and they would combine for a 27% share.
Here's a look at Paramount Skydance's full statement on the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 states earlier this week:
The complaint filed by the state attorneys general in federal district court in the Northern District of California distorts settled antitrust law and is based on a misrepresentation of competition in the entertainment industry today. As numerous antitrust authorities around the world have already concluded after months of review, this transaction creates a stronger competitor against dominant streaming and technology platforms who have harmed the market for theatrical exhibition and jobs in the entertainment industry. This merger will create a company capable of investing more aggressively in premium content, theatrical releases, and creative talent at a time when those investments matter more than ever.
"The lawsuit filed by the state attorneys general, in the most generous light, reflects a fundamentally flawed application of the antitrust laws and is wrong on both the facts and the law. We will vigorously defend the transaction and demonstrate that this challenge is inconsistent with sound competition policy and the competitive realities of the media marketplace. Delaying this transaction will only harm entertainment workers who have already suffered over recent years as technology has disrupted their livelihood and cost California tens of thousands of entertainment jobs."
"The combination of Paramount and WBD will create a stronger, well-capitalized, creative-first media company that is better positioned to compete with companies like Netflix that have come to dominate the industry for audiences, premium content, and creative talent. Put simply, any attempt to block this transaction undermines the very principles antitrust law is designed to promote: more competition, more choice for consumers, and more opportunities for creators and workers," according to a Paramount spokesperson.
"The practical effect of this lawsuit is to shield those dominant streaming platforms like Netflix and technology companies from much needed competition while preventing the significant benefits this transaction will deliver for consumers, creators, workers, and the broader Hollywood economy. We will continue to fight against any attempt to derail a deal that strengthens competition, expands opportunity, and positions the combined company to compete in an increasingly competitive global media landscape," the spokesperson said.
Competition and FDI Regulators in 24 Jurisdictions Have Cleared the Transaction
The regulators that have reviewed the transaction have cleared it or allowed the waiting periods to expire, underscoring the deal's lack of anticompetitive effects on the industry. For example, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found that: "[T]he Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in relation to the wholesale supply of films for theatrical release in Australia." The ACCC expressly noted that while "the Acquisition would remove competition between Paramount and Warner Brothers, the merged entity would continue to be constrained by other film studios post-Acquisition" and "[t]he materials do not support the view that Paramount and Warner Brothers are particularly close competitors or that they compete more closely with each other than with the other major film studios." The U.S. Department of Justice reached a similar conclusion when it closed its merger investigation.
In addition to the United States, competition regulators around the world have concluded that the merger will not pose any threat to competition. Paramount has received competition clearances in Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), Kuwait, Montenegro, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, South Korea, and Ukraine. Paramount has also received foreign direct investment (FDI) clearances in Australia, Germany, France, Spain, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, New Zealand, Italy, and Romania.
The careful review undertaken by these regulators and their uniform decision to clear the transaction or allow it to proceed contrasts sharply with the approach taken by the state attorneys general in this case. We will fight any effort to block a merger that has clear benefits for consumers, creators, and the wider entertainment industry, and where the alternative is to entrench a failing status quo.
Paramount Has Consistently Demonstrated How the Transaction Benefits Workers, Creators, and Theaters
Throughout the merger review process, Paramount has consistently demonstrated to enforcement bodies and other key stakeholders how this transaction will strengthen—not weaken—the creative economy.
Paramount CEO David Ellison has been clear since announcing the transaction that it will benefit consumers, theater exhibitors and creatives alike, because Paramount will release at least 30 high-quality films annually for full theatrical exhibition with a minimum 45-day window and continue licensing content to and acquiring content from third parties. In a May 7, 2026 letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Paramount explained that Netflix, Amazon, and Disney are the largest subscription streaming services by far, that Paramount and WBD "lack the scale to compete effectively against the leading SVODs," and that, "[a]bsent something transformative, neither party is positioned to grow to a scale where they would catch up to the leading streamers." Later, in a May 28, 2026 letter to the Attorney General, Paramount expanded on that point by explaining why the transaction's output-enhancing strategy is central to competing at scale, noting that "the proposed transaction will increase output, expand theatrical releases, and enhance competition with scaled streaming platforms, all of which depend on sustained and growing demand for creative talent," and made clear the economic logic behind the deal: "A firm seeking to grow market share against larger competitors, including the streaming giants, must invest in more and better content and talent, not cut."
Paramount also has detailed how this transaction will help workers rather than continue to subject them to a failing Hollywood system. In a June 5, 2026 letter to the Department of Justice responding to a white paper submitted by the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Paramount explained how "[its] content strategy aligns directly with the Teamsters' interests. More films and series in production means more call sheets, more location days, more transportation, casting, and catering work." As Paramount observed, "[t]he combined company will have no incentive to shrink the production engine that drives its competitiveness. Increasing production volume is the central pillar of how Paramount intends to compete." Moreover, "[i]nvigorated competition to produce more content across the entertainment industry will translate to more opportunities for organized labor beyond Paramount's projects." Ultimately, "Paramount cannot enhance and expand content production without organized labor" and "the Teamsters and other unions will stand as must-have partners for Paramount for years to come."
results.summary:
Paramount Skydance and a coalition of 12 states are currently deadlocked over the trial date for the antitrust lawsuit challenging the proposed merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.

### Key Points
- Paramount Skydance has requested a November 4, 2026, trial date, while a coalition of 12 states led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta is pushing for April 5, 2027.
- The lawsuit alleges the merger violates Section 7 of the Clayton Act by reducing competition in theatrical film distribution and basic cable television licensing.
- State attorneys general argue the consolidation will lead to higher consumer prices, reduced content quality, and fewer opportunities for entertainment industry workers.
- Paramount maintains the merger is pro-competitive, arguing it provides the necessary scale to compete against dominant streaming platforms like Netflix and major tech companies.
- International regulators in 24 jurisdictions, including Australia and Canada, have already cleared the transaction, finding it unlikely to substantially lessen market competition.

### Why it Matters
The scheduling dispute carries significant financial weight, as Paramount Skydance could face substantial daily shareholder liabilities if the legal process extends beyond September 2026. This case serves as a critical test for media consolidation, pitting state-level antitrust enforcement against the industry's push for greater scale to survive in a streaming-dominated market.

results.title: TSLL: How Tesla Investors Lose Money Even When the Stock Goes Up
results.author: Ryne Mauck
results.content:
The Direxion Daily TSLA Bull 2X Shares ETF (NASDAQ:TSLL) promises to deliver twice Tesla’s daily returns, making it an appealing choice for investors looking to amplify gains in one of the market’s most volatile stocks. However, many investors overlook one critical detail: TSLL is built to track Tesla’s daily performance, not its long-term returns.
That distinction matters. Tesla has historically experienced enormous price swings, including multiple declines of 40% or more followed by powerful recoveries. While long-term Tesla shareholders have often been rewarded for staying invested, those same swings can work against leveraged ETFs because of their daily reset mechanism. Over weeks or months, TSLL can lose value even if Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA | TSLA Price Prediction) ultimately finishes higher.
Before buying TSLL, it is crucial that investors understand how Tesla’s volatility interacts with leveraged ETF mechanics. In many cases, the biggest risk isn’t simply that Tesla stock price falls; instead, it’s that the stock becomes too volatile, even while trending upward.
Tesla’s Stock is Defined by Its Volatility
Tesla has been one of the stock market’s biggest success stories over the past decade. Since its 2010 IPO, the stock has generated gains of well over 20,000%, going from a relatively small EV manufacturer into one of the world’s most valuable companies. Long-term shareholders who held throughout all of the volatility have been rewarded with extraordinary returns.
However, those gains have come with equally extraordinary price swings. Tesla has experienced multiple drawdowns exceeding 40%, including a decline of roughly 74% between November 2021 and January 2023 before eventually recovering to new highs. Even during strong bull markets, double-digit moves over a matter of days or weeks have been common for the stock, making Tesla one of the most volatile mega-cap stocks in the market.
This volatility is precisely why leveraged ETFs such as TSLL behave differently than the underlying stock itself. Large daily price swings can cause returns to diverge over time, meaning investors may not receive twice Tesla’s long-term performance, even when the stock ultimately trends higher (a phenomenon known as volatility decay).
How TSLL’s Leverage Mechanics Could Lose You Money
TSLL seeks to deliver 200% of Tesla’s daily performance, resetting its leverage at the close of every trading session. That daily reset is what allows the fund to maintain its 2x target, but it also means returns can compound differently than the underlying stock over longer holding periods.
In steadily rising markets, TSLL can outperform by magnifying Tesla’s gains. Whereas in volatile and/or choppy sideways markets it’s a different story. When Tesla experiences large gains followed by large losses, or vice versa, TSLL must continually rebalance its exposure. This “buy high, sell low” effect can gradually erode returns.
For that reason, TSLL is generally designed for short-term tactical trading rather than long-term investing. Investors who expect to hold TSLL for years may find that simply owning the underlying asset (TSLA) produces far better long-term performance. The data supports this.
Key Fund Statistics
Before investing in any leveraged ETF, it is important to understand the fund’s structure, costs, and objective. The following statistics provide a quick overview of TSLL and highlight several key characteristics that differentiate it from a traditional ETF.
| Metric | TSLL | 
| Underlying Asset | Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) | 
| Inception Date | August 9, 2022 | 
| Investment Objective | 200% of Tesla’s daily return | 
| Rebalance Frequency | Daily | 
| Net Assets | $3.00B | 
| Expense Ratio | 0.83% | 
| YTD Total Return | -62.00% (Compared to -31.64% for TSLA) | 
| 1-year Total Return | -36.80% (Compared to -5.57% for TSLA) | 
| 3-year Cumulative Return | -53.10% (Compared to +15.39% for TSLA) | 
| 5-year Cumulative Return | -65.18% (Compared to +42.56% for TSLA) | 
| Max Historical Drawdown | -82.88% | 
Final Takeaway
TSLL can be a powerful trading tool, but it is not simply a faster version of owning Tesla stock. Because the fund resets its leverage daily, long-term returns can dramatically differ from Tesla’s own performance, particularly during periods of elevated volatility. As the historical data shows, investors who held TSLL over extended periods have often significantly underperformed those who simply owned shares directly in Tesla.
For most long-term investors, buying Tesla directly is likely the better choice. TSLL is best suited for traders with a short-term strong-conviction outlook that the stock is going to meaningfully move higher.

### Key Points

Leveraged ETFs like TSLL are complex financial instruments that behave differently than the underlying assets they track over extended timeframes. Investors who mistake these products for long-term investment vehicles risk substantial capital loss due to the mathematical impact of daily volatility resets.

results.title: Your Roku could be stuck at 1080p and you’d never know
results.author: Chris Hachey
results.content:
There was a famous infomercial in the late 1990s in the U.S. about the Ronco Showtime Rotisserie. The pitchman would talk about how you could load up the cooking machine with food and then "set it and forget it." That motto and principle have been used in tech for years, as devices want to make it easy on the users. They don't want them to worry about making adjustments by making the factory settings good enough for most people.
Unfortunately, for consumers, sometimes this isn't the best thing. In fact, anybody who has adjusted the settings of their computer, headphones, or other electronic devices knows that there are plenty of changes you can make to better your experience. The same goes for a Roku. Because if you don't take a look, "setting it and forgetting it" might give you a worse experience.
There are a ton of settings you can change on a Roku
You need to do some digging
Roku OS is known as a user-friendly device that makes it easy for consumers to get the content they want. The grid-style design has been upgraded recently to take your preferences and offer you suggestions based on those. While you may not want Roku to track your activity, if you do use the algorithm the way it's intended, it will give you recommendations for content.
For those who don't want to be tracked, you can go into the Settings menu to stop it. Opting to hide Roku's recommendations is even just a way to get rid of them on your main screen.
You can also use the Settings menu to save power on your device. You can stop the auto-play of videos on the home screen with just the click of a button. Your viewing can be smoother if you're experiencing any difficulty with the picture. Just going to Advanced display settings and adjusting the refresh rate will improve your picture.
Roku even lets you choose what your captions look like when you're streaming content and want to use subtitles. It's worth looking around to see how best your Roku can serve you and your TV.
Different Roku devices might have slightly different settings menus. If you have an older Streaming Stick or a newer Roku Ultra, you might see that the options are different, solely based on the technological advancements made between products. When it comes to software changes, as long as the Roku is updated, they will be the same.
You can change the display type of your Roku
This should match the resolution of your TV
On one TV in my home, I have an older Roku Streaming Stick that I've had for years. On another, I have a newer Roku Streaming Stick. The green displays are from the older TV and the Roku Streaming Stick. The purple photos are from the newer TV and Streaming Stick. Neither of the TVs is a smart TV on its own.
You can change the display type on your Roku so it better matches the resolution that your TV can show. To do so, you must go to Settings and then Display type. You'll see several display options that Roku can default to.
Rokus are set to choose the standard option that your TV allows. For both of my TVs, this is 1080p. I do have the option to choose 720p if I want though. I don't mind 1080p on these TVs at all as it is high definition viewing, which is just fine for me. Both of these TVs are in bedrooms, so I don't need the best viewing capabilities. We're usually just watching the news or streaming a show on Netflix or Disney+ from bed when using any of them.
I do have a Samsung Frame TV downstairs that supports 4K HDR but I don't usually use my Roku with that. When I did plug in the Roku to the One Connect box, it allowed me to choose any of these other options.
Why you might want to change it
There are reasons why you might not to
If you're watching something specifically, like streaming a sporting event, you might want to go with the higher 4K option or even the 1080p if you have been watching in 720p. This will provide you with clearer visuals and help you watch something in better detail.
It's also smart to use a higher option, such as 4K HDR, if you're watching a movie that could benefit from the brightest colors. I like to rely on something like Filmmaker Mode and turn off things such as motion smoothing to give me the best picture while watching on my big TV.
Shows and movies with dramatic light and intense visuals are worth putting in the better display types. If you want to get the most out of your TV, you can do so by switching this on your Roku.
You might want to save your bandwidth though, which is used up exponentially more when you're streaming in 4K compared to HD. If you have a lot of devices connected to your Wi-Fi alongside your Roku device, it could cause your network to slow down considerably.
There's also the argument that streaming in 4K compresses the audio and video too much, and it doesn't show it in as natural of a format as HD does. This is where a debate about physical media versus streaming can come into play.
Make sure you're comfortable with Roku's choice of display type
Your Roku device will automatically choose what display type to use to stream your content. It's a simple choice to change it, as you just need to scroll in the Settings menu and select a new one if you want to switch. You can do this manually based on what you're watching or just rely on Roku to do it for you. How much involvement you want is entirely up to you.
Roku Ultra (2024)
The Roku Ultra (2024) offers new capabilities for streaming devices. It has Wi-Fi 6 connectivity, a lost remote feature, and a faster processor speed than its predecessors. The voice remote has backlit buttons for easier use in the dark.
results.summary:
Roku users can significantly improve their streaming experience and device performance by manually adjusting hidden settings rather than relying on the default factory configurations provided by the manufacturer.

### Key Points
- Users can navigate to the Settings menu to disable activity tracking, hide content recommendations, and stop home screen video auto-play.
- Adjusting the "Display type" in settings allows users to match the Roku output to their specific TV resolution, such as 720p, 1080p, or 4K HDR.
- Advanced display settings enable manual refresh rate adjustments to resolve picture quality issues during playback.
- Customization options extend to subtitle appearance and power-saving modes to optimize the device for individual preferences.
- The 2024 Roku Ultra features hardware upgrades including Wi-Fi 6 connectivity, a faster processor, and a backlit voice remote.

### Why it Matters
Default settings often prioritize convenience over performance, potentially limiting the visual quality or privacy of the streaming experience. Taking control of these configurations ensures that users maximize their hardware capabilities while managing bandwidth consumption effectively.

results.title: Windows has been quietly wearing out your SSD, and the fix takes one setting
results.author: Abhinav Raj
results.content:
It's hard to imagine that, just a little over a year ago, a dead SSD used to be an $80 or $100 bill. Today, replacing that same 1TB drive has become close to a $220 problem. It was, after all, this number that changed how seriously I was looking at my NVMe's lifespan, especially since that's something I hadn't considered at all.
Now, I've never been the type to baby my hardware, but watching NAND prices climb has me looking twice at anything that shortens my Gen 4 NVME's lifespan for any reason. The problem is that I've grown accustomed to trusting Windows to be a sensible custodian of my hardware, and more often than not, it just isn't. Some of its defaults were clearly designed for an era of spinning HDDs that don't exist in many builds like mine. I found one of those troublemaking "defaults" on my own PC, writing gigabytes worth of data on every single shutdown. Here's what it is.
My PC hadn't properly "shut down" in years
Fast Startup happens to be just hibernation in disguise
When you click Shut Down on your Windows 11 PC, your PC doesn't really shut down, at least, not in the way you'd expect it to. What the system does is basically log you out, take a snapshot of the kernel (which manages your hardware and anything running on top) along with your loaded drivers, compresses that snapshot, and writes it to a hidden file on your main boot drive (usually C: for most users) called hiberfil.sys. The next time you power on, Windows reads that file back into memory. This saves quite a bit of time, and that's why it's aptly named Fast Startup. It's a form of hibernation running behind the scenes on every shutdown, whether you asked for it or not.
I came across this accidentally while going through a disk-space audit on my machine, wondering why my NVMe, which should have plenty of headroom, kept feeling tighter than it should, while installing some local AI models. With a quick scan via WizTree (a utility that maps what's exactly eating your storage), I found a 12.5GB hiberfil.sys file in sight, sitting as one of the largest single files on my entire drive.
What does it cost you?
A lot of wear over time, and a decent chunk of space
Every shutdown and restart writes this hiberfil.sys snapshot to your drive, typically sized to match your installed RAM. To be fair, this alone won't kill a healthy SSD. Against a typical drive's rated endurance of several hundred TBW (Terabytes Written), this amount of writing seems fairly small. The problem is the fact that, over time, these become thousands of writes over the drive's working life, and every single one of them is avoidable. The entire process is only buying you a couple of seconds that you likely won't notice.
Another problem is that this gets worse on a fuller drive, since an SSD with less free space has less room for its controller to work with during garbage collection, and that raises write amplification, which means the same hiberfil.sys write causes more wear on a drive that's 95% full than it would on a relatively empty one.
Although it may be a minor gripe, there's also the issue of the space this file occupies. My hiberfil.sys file ballooned up to 12.5GB, and if I were to pair that up with pagefile.sys, the total storage occupied accounts for 24GB of lost capacity, which isn't doing me any good. On space-constrained systems, I can see that being an issue, particularly because there are still budget laptops shipping with 512 GB of usable storage.
Should you turn it off?
It's worth a thought for laptop owners
There is an option to keep hibernation intact and switch off Fast Startup. If you open the Control Panel, go into Power Options, and then select, "Choose what the power buttons do", you might notice the checkbox is greyed out. You'd have to click, "Change settings that are currently unavailable" above it, and then untick "Turn on fast startup", and simply save. Your shutdowns from this point on will actually shut down your PC, although the hiberfil.sys file will stay put.
The other option will help you reclaim the disk space for you. You can right-click Start, open Terminal as an Administrator, and type powercfg /h off, and then hit Enter. This will delete the hiberfil.sys file and hands you back the space. In my case, it was about 12.5GB. It's worth noting that this is a fully supported Microsoft command and not a hack. It's also reversible with the same command, you'd just have to substitute "off" with "on."
Laptop owners do have a little something to think about when following these steps, though. Hibernation saves your session if the battery gives out, and using powercfg /h off gets rid of that safety net if you were relying on it. If that describes you, the option of the two is the safer pick, since it saves your SSD from the wrath of Fast Startup's daily writes while leaving Hibernate available when you choose to trigger it manually.
My SSD finally gets some rest
Fast Startup isn't really a feature that you need to rush out and disable right away, and your SSD endurance will likely be fine for a while. The actual problem is the cost of replacement down the line, and when replacing a 1TB NVMe now costs double what it used to, avoiding unnecessary writes and reclaiming a fair amount of storage feels right to me.
results.summary:
Windows 11 users can extend the lifespan of their NVMe SSDs and reclaim significant storage space by disabling the Fast Startup feature, which performs unnecessary daily drive writes.

### Key Points
- Fast Startup creates a large hiberfil.sys file on the boot drive every time a computer shuts down, consuming gigabytes of storage capacity.
- Frequent writing to the hiberfil.sys file contributes to cumulative wear on SSDs, which is increasingly concerning as replacement costs for 1TB drives have doubled.
- Users can disable Fast Startup via the Control Panel or permanently remove the hiberfil.sys file by running the "powercfg /h off" command in an Administrator Terminal.
- Disabling hibernation removes a safety net for laptop users, as the system will no longer save the current session if the battery completely depletes.
- SSDs with less free space experience higher write amplification, making the removal of large, unnecessary system files beneficial for drive health and performance.

### Why it Matters
Rising NAND flash prices have made SSD longevity a significant financial concern for PC owners looking to maximize their hardware's lifespan. By disabling unnecessary background processes like Fast Startup, users can reduce avoidable wear and reclaim valuable storage space on their primary drives.

results.title: Poll: Majority of Americans Distrust AI in Workplace, Cite Job Security Concerns
results.author: Chase Codewell
results.content:
The findings align with warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which stated in a June report that AI is likely to abolish a range of jobs and "raise profound concerns about massive labor disruptions and rising inequality" [3]. A Goldman Sachs report cited that approximately one-quarter of all white-collar jobs are at risk of being replaced by AI, affecting fields such as customer service, legal work, and journalism [4]. These reports indicate that distrust over AI's impact on employment extends well beyond younger workers.
The Gallup survey showed that younger members of Generation Z who are still in K-12 education were more likely than older Gen Z adults to say they use AI at least weekly, yet distrust remained high across the age group [1]. While the poll focused on younger respondents, the Goldman Sachs report indicates that white-collar roles—often held by college-educated workers—are particularly vulnerable to automation [4].
The International Monetary Fund warned that AI's impact will be felt across skill levels, potentially increasing inequality, and urged governments to prepare for labor disruptions [3]. These patterns suggest that distrust is not confined to any single demographic but is widespread among workers whose jobs face potential automation.
Job displacement is the most cited fear, according to multiple reports. The great AI displacement has already begun, with major companies like Amazon and Nestlé cutting thousands of jobs due to AI, uniquely targeting white-collar and cognitive roles, according to a November 2025 article [5]. In October 2025 alone, U.S. employers announced 153,074 job cuts, the highest for that month in more than two decades, with the technology sector accounting for over 33,000 layoffs, driven by corporate cost-cutting and AI adoption [6].
Data privacy and algorithmic bias are additional sources of concern. Dr. Subhash Kak, a computing expert at Oklahoma University, said that employment gives people a "sense of self-worth and value," but warned that technological advances can take that away [7]. Venture capitalist Marc Andreessen has argued that plummeting wages driven by AI are a necessary step toward a consumer paradise, a view critics say could create a dystopian underclass [8]. The IMF has called for expanded unemployment insurance to address these disruptions [3].
Some technology companies defend AI adoption, stating that AI can augment rather than replace human labor. A November 2025 report noted that autonomous AI systems are set to become ubiquitous, handling tasks like scheduling and health monitoring, while demand for human data analysts is expected to grow as AI takes over analytical roles [13]. Digital entrepreneur Dan Golka discussed launching an open-source AI model called Enoch to assist business managers with automated tasks, reflecting industry efforts toward integration [9].
Critics, however, argue that the pace of automation outpaces regulatory safeguards. In an interview, Mike Adams noted that AI models have "the potential to replace up to 50% of desk jobs in the coming years," emphasizing the need for human adaptation [10]. The book "Human + Machine" by Paul R. Daugherty and H. James Wilson suggests that AI's impact is more about job transformation than elimination, with humans freed to focus on complex and creative work, but acknowledges that generative AI has dramatically heightened fears of replacement [11]. The IMF has urged governments to expand unemployment insurance and retraining programs [3].
The poll underscores a persistent gap between corporate AI ambitions and public trust, according to analysts. The International Monetary Fund has called for expanded unemployment insurance and retraining programs to mitigate disruption [3]. The book "AI: Unlocking the Future" by K. Connors emphasizes the need for investment in education and workforce retraining to equip workers for an AI-driven economy [12].
Future policy and industry efforts may need to address transparency, retraining, and worker participation to shift perceptions. As one expert noted in the Goldman Sachs report, many workers view AI as a technology that could make arbitrary decisions about hiring and firing, highlighting the need for safeguards.
results.summary:
Widespread public distrust regarding artificial intelligence persists as reports from the International Monetary Fund and Goldman Sachs highlight significant risks of job displacement and rising economic inequality.

### Key Points
- Goldman Sachs estimates that approximately one-quarter of all white-collar jobs, including legal and journalism roles, are at risk of replacement by AI.
- U.S. employers announced 153,074 job cuts in October 2025, with the technology sector contributing over 33,000 layoffs driven by AI adoption and cost-cutting.
- The International Monetary Fund warns that AI-driven labor disruptions could increase inequality and recommends that governments expand unemployment insurance and worker retraining programs.
- Major corporations, including Amazon and Nestlé, have already begun cutting thousands of positions as they transition toward automated and cognitive-based AI systems.
- Experts like Mike Adams suggest that AI models could potentially replace up to 50% of desk jobs, fueling concerns about algorithmic bias and data privacy.

### Why it Matters
The rapid integration of AI into the workforce is creating a significant disconnect between corporate efficiency goals and public job security. Addressing these concerns through policy, such as expanded social safety nets and workforce retraining, is essential to mitigate the potential for widespread economic instability.

results.title: I electrocuted my own vagus nerve every day for a week to find out if brain health wearables are worth the hype
results.author: matt.evans@futurenet.com (Matt Evans) , Matt Evans
results.content:
You could be forgiven for thinking that most wearable-tech categories have come as far as they're ever going to. All smartwatches look the same now, and that form factor isn’t going away anytime soon. It's a similar story with smart rings, with “slightly thinner” being the main selling point of the Oura Ring 5. And the screenless Whoop tracker has given birth to a bunch of copycats, including the Fitbit Air, and most recently the Garmin Cirqa.
When you think of wearable tech, you normally think of some sort of fitness tracker. But there is an area of wearables that’s still in flux, as categories do before there’s a consensus on what works: neurotech. Neurotech devices are generally wearable technology to monitor, or temporarily alter, our brain chemistry for optimal performance or to treat neurological injuries, such as post-traumatic stress disorder or depression.
They’re also being used to improve our brains to rest harder and focus longer. Our writer Becca Caddy recently wrote about the dangerously addictive thrills of 'over-optimization', so it’s no surprise to see the out-there concept of rewiring the brain being embraced by the cult of biohacking.
Nootropics — mind-enhancing drugs — are promoted heavily on podcasts, with brands like Gorilla Mind and Alpha Brain enjoying airtime on popular ‘bro-science’ platforms like The Joe Rogan Experience to help get ‘cognitively dialed’. Away from pharmacological solutions, multi-millionaire longevity biohacker Bryan Johnson uses Nurosym, an electrical vagus nerve stimulation device, to “make [his] body more parasympathetic, more chill”.
It’s Nurosym that I’ve been using this week. There are other wearables out there that promise to do all sorts of things — the Neurosity Crown for example (pictured above), promises to improve concentration through “neuroadaptive meditation”, measuring your brainwaves and playing music to that pattern to improve focus during work. All while looking like the sort of thing you might see Patrick Stewart wear in the X-Men films.
The Muse 2 headband is a meditation aid that uses electroencephalography (EEG) sensors to read your brain activity and provide personalized meditation guidance, in much the same way as a smartwatch might read your heart rate and offer workout suggestions.
The vagus nerve, however, is a key target for brain health. Proper stimulation of the vagus nerve is said to offer all sorts of benefits, treating conditions as varied as depression, anxiety, inflammation, bipolar disorder, obesity, POTS, and Alzheimer's. For people without those conditions, vagus nerve stimulation can improve sleep quality, regulate stress and improve relaxation overall, ensuring you're well-rested and ready to tackle life's challenges.

There's unconfirmed but promising research suggesting that you may be able to stimulate the vagus nerve yourself through practices such as meditation and cold exposure — which might explain my predilection for cold showers, as perhaps I’ve been unconsciously hacking away at my brain all this time.
But what if I got a wearable to do it for me? I decided to try Nurosym myself for a week, to see if I could really begin to hack my brain better.
The vagus nerve stimulation device costs a whopping $699 / £599 (around AU$1,300), and looks quite stripped-back for a device of this price. It consists of a fairly simple handheld remote, an attached earpiece with a clamp to fix to your tragus (the small piece of cartilage outside your ear) and a charging cable. There’s mercifully no app or phone connection to speak of; everything happens on-device, which actually goes some way to making me trust it more, as it’s not collecting any data about me.
“For a long time, neuromodulation has largely meant invasive procedures or treatment delivered in specialist environments,” Dr Greta Dalle Luche, PhD., Nurosym’s head of science, tells me. “Nurosym demonstrates how this science can be translated into non-invasive technology that fits into people’s everyday lives.”
As well as being a doctor in biochemistry, Dalle Luche is also a former professional surfer, so she knows all about optimizing for peak performance. She explains that Nurosym is all about taking “evidence-led neuromodulation” out of the clinical space and turning it into accessible technology. A lot of clinical tests have been done on this device, and it’s advertised as “the world’s most studied vagus nerve stimulator” with $10 million invested in over 60 independent research papers, backed by notable universities and health bodies worldwide.
To use it, you moisten your tragus, fix the clamp, then adjust the signal on the remote — turning it up until you feel a light tingling sensation. That’s the electricity pulsing through your ear to your vagus nerve, stimulating the parasympathetic nervous system to activate your body’s “rest and digest” response.
It seems like as good a place as any to start. I wet my ear, clamped it onto myself and sat quietly, letting the tingles of electricity wash down my ear canal and into my brain. Nurosym guidelines, and reports on the r/vagusnerve subreddit (because of course there’s a subreddit), suggest that it can take anything from a few days to months to feel the effects, which are said to include a reduction in depressive or anxiety-related symptoms, better sleep, and better-quality rest and relaxation. These claims are anecdotal, and user-dependent, and the results are subjective, with no objective measure of they actually work or produce meaningful results, certainly in a short amount of time such as a week.
Dalle Luche tells me that “factors such as an individual’s underlying vagal tone, or in other words, the ‘health of their autonomic nervous system,’ influence the proportion of the response to the device". So it's possible that I may end up not having a proportional, or significant, response.
Nonetheless, I did my best to empirically measure my body’s responses to this new technology, monitoring my sessions on a Garmin Cirqa fitness tracker as if it was a workout, and wearing it to bed nightly to monitor sleep quality and heart-rate variability.
You can watch our video review of the Garmin Cirqa below:
According to the Garmin, the stimulation did have some effect. There could be any number of contributing factors for this, but after spending 15 minutes at rest to settle my heart, I fired up the Nurosym and monitored my heart rate over a 25-minute session, and I did see a decrease in spikes my heart rate as the session went on. Note the regularity in the middle there, too, between the 10 and 17-minute marks — a clear indication that something was working.
Across the week while using the device, I also saw a general improvement in sleep quality and drastically rising heart-rate variability, as measured here via my Garmin. I’m not sure I saw any immediate, dramatic improvement in focus or relaxation, but the graphs were moving in the right direction.
Whether this is partly due to the sessions enforcing at least 30 minutes of screenless, conscious relaxation time each day, so that my nervous system was deliberately being calmed, or whether it’s due to the device, I’m not sure. But I’ll take the W, as the kids say.
For $700 / £600 / AU$1,300, is 'seemed to work' enough? When I asked about the high price of the device, Nurosym’s head of science Dr Greta Dalle Luche said its price does not reflect the physical device alone.
“It reflects more than a decade of scientific research and development, our proprietary technology, extensive continuous testing to ensure safety and maintenance of regulatory certification, as well as continued investment in clinical research,” she told me. “That makes a direct product-for-product comparison with lower-cost non-validated wellness gadgets difficult.
“When people buy Nurosym, they have the certainty of holding in their hands something that works, and that comes with very little risk.”
While the results have been inconclusive so far, I've seen enough to suggest that something is happening here, so I'll continue electrocuting my brain for a while yet to see if I achieve more definitive results. Wearable neurotechnology is still in its infancy, but it’s a technology that's on the rise, and I imagine, now that Nurosym has done the hard work of all that proprietary testing, there will be more low-strength vagus nerve-stimulation devices hitting the market in the near future.
I’m interested in seeing where the category goes. If companies like Nurosym can bring down prices, and make the technology more accessible, a wearable that improves your quality of relaxation — and which doesn’t harvest your data to feed big tech via an AI-powered app — sounds like a win in my book.

A former staffer at Men's Health, he holds a Master's Degree in journalism from Cardiff and has written for brands like Runner's World, Women's Health, Men's Fitness, LiveScience and Fit&Well on everything fitness tech, exercise, nutrition and mental wellbeing.
Matt's a keen runner, ex-kickboxer, not averse to the odd yoga flow, and insists everyone should stretch every morning. When he’s not training or writing about health and fitness, he can be found reading doorstop-thick fantasy books with lots of fictional maps in them.

results.summary:
The emerging field of neurotech is expanding beyond fitness tracking as devices like the Nurosym vagus nerve stimulator aim to improve brain health and relaxation through non-invasive electrical stimulation.

### Key Points
- Nurosym is a $699 wearable device that uses electrical pulses on the tragus to stimulate the vagus nerve and activate the body's "rest and digest" response.
- The technology is marketed as an evidence-led alternative to clinical neuromodulation, backed by over 60 independent research papers and $10 million in investment.
- Other neurotech wearables include the Neurosity Crown for focus and the Muse 2 headband for meditation, both utilizing brainwave monitoring.
- Potential benefits of vagus nerve stimulation include reduced anxiety, improved sleep quality, and better heart-rate variability.
- Critics and users note that results are subjective, and the high cost of current devices remains a significant barrier to mainstream adoption.

### Why it Matters
Neurotech represents a shift in wearable technology from passive data collection to active physiological intervention. As these devices move from clinical settings to consumer markets, they offer new ways to manage stress and mental performance, though they raise questions about long-term efficacy and accessibility.
